newsitem.title: GERMANY: Analysts see no inflation risk in German data.
newsitem.headline: Analysts see no inflation risk in German data.

text.p: German wholesale prices posted their first year-on-year rise in 13 months in October, data on Tuesday showed, but analysts said inflation pressures were in abeyance despite a jump in oil prices.
The Federal Statistics Office said wholesale prices rose by 0.2 percent in October against September, when they fell by 0.1 percent.

Wholesale prices rose by 0.9 percent against the same month a year earlier, after falling by 0.7 percent in September. But the latest jump was mainly due to the statistical impact of a sharp price drop in October 1995.
"From our point of view this is not an early inflation indicator," Ralf Kugelstadt of UBS in Frankfurt told Reuters.
Peter Pietsch of Commerzbank agreed: "I can't imagine that anyone can be worried about wholesale prices...It is one of the few good indicators in a rather gloomy economic picture."
Analysts agreed that the price climate was benign and the latest data had no implications for monetary policy -- with the Bundesbank watching the pace of German recovery more closely than prices.
Pietsch said that, after sluggish industrial data last week, there was still a slight chance of a further easing in rates but added a period of rate stability was more likely.

Key components of the wholesale price index driving the month-on-month rise in October were heating oil, up 13 percent and diesel fuel, up 6.8 percent. Motor gasoline, however, was up just 0.9 percent.
